newsitem.title: USA: Silicon Graphics shines, brightens Wall Street.
newsitem.headline: Silicon Graphics shines, brightens Wall Street.

text.p: Silicon Graphics Inc. shares dazzled Wall Street with its own special effects Friday, soaring 31 percent after the graphics computer maker posted surprisingly strong fiscal 1997 results.
Stock in the Mountain View, Calif.-based company rose $5.875 to close at $25.31 on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the fourth most active share on volume of 9.6 million.

The company, whose products are used in computer-intensive applications ranging from complex weather modeling to special effects for Hollywood movies, issued an earnings report late Thursday that startled analysts after nearly two years of repeated quarterly shortfalls.
"The company executed far better on the quarter than they had any time on the prior six quarters," said Jay Stevens, an analyst at Buckingham Research in New York.

Silicon Graphics reported net income of $102 million, or 56 cents a share, on sales of $1.2 billion. A year earlier, the company posted a loss of $48.7 million, or 30 cents a share, on sales of $977 million.
The profit, announced after the close of Thursday's market trading, easily beat the 34 cents a share that Wall Street analysts surveyed by First Call had expected.

In addition, Chief Executive Officer Edward McCracken said in an interview Thursday that he expects Silicon Graphics to be able to sustain the higher profit margins it achieved in the latest quarter throughout its 1998 fiscal year.
More than half a dozen prominent Wall Street analysts recommended that investors buy shares in the company, raising fiscal 1998 earnings estimates by up to 20 percent.

Bear Stearns, Cowen & Co., Goldman Sachs, Hambrecht & Quist, ABN AMRO Chicago Corp., Salomon Brothers and Buckingham all raised their rating for Silicon Graphics stock to attractive from neutral or "market perform" ratings.

The favorable earnings report gave Silicon Graphics investors a welcome boost after a sweeping product transition over the last year contributed to repeated earnings disappointments and battered the company's shares.

Analysts said it should boost morale for management and employees after a very difficult year of ramping up production of an entirely new product line while absorbing supercomputer maker Cray Research, which it bought in April 1996.
"You get your head beat in for six months in a row and you begin to wonder if you've lost your grip," said Stevens. "It might be a rebulding of confidence they can do this."
McCracken said the fourth quarter demonstrated the company can carry through with its business and manufacturing plans now that all the new products are in full production.
"Our product transition is complete, we are shipping our entire product line...and, most importantly, the new products are finding strong acceptance with customers," he said.
For the year, Silicon Graphics earned $78.5 million, or 43 cents a share, on sales of $3.09 billion. A year earlier, the company earned $115 million, or 65 cents a share, on sales of $2.55 billion.

Several analysts commented on the timing of a cover story in next week's Business Week, available on its Web site Friday, saying it was inauspicously entitled "The Sad Saga of Silicon Graphics" just as the company is rebounding.

But one analyst noted the business weekly had published a favorable piece about Silicon Graphics, which it dubbed "the gee-whiz company," three years ago, around the time the stock hit its all time high of $46.625 in mid-1995.
